title: Start Early
concept: Starting to invest earlier gives money more time to grow and potentially earn returns on previous growth.
learningObjective: Understand how starting earlier can improve long-term investment outcomes by giving money more time to grow.
primaryMisconception: Starting later with more money always makes it easy to catch up with someone who started earlier.
secondaryMisconceptions: Small amounts invested early cannot make a meaningful difference.
The amount invested matters, but the length of time invested does not.
keyTakeaway: Time can be one of the strongest advantages in long-term investing.

screens.title: A Ten-Year Head Start
screens.content: Two friends invest £100 monthly. One starts ten years earlier. At 60, who contributed more—and who may finish with more?
screens.illustration: Two runners follow the same long timeline. One starts at age 20, while the other waits at the age-30 marker.

screens.title: Same Goal, Different Start
screens.content: Hana starts investing £100 monthly at age 20. Omar plans to invest the same amount but waits until age 30.
screens.illustration: Hana begins at the age-20 marker while Omar’s path remains paused until age 30.

screens.title: Ten Years Already Working
screens.content: When Omar begins, Hana has already made ten years of contributions. Her earlier money has also had time for possible growth.
screens.illustration: Hana’s timeline shows contributions and a separate growth layer. Omar’s timeline begins at zero.

screens.title: Growth on Earlier Growth
screens.content: Both continue contributing. Over time, Hana’s earlier returns may generate additional returns, increasing the value of her head start.
screens.illustration: Small growth branches appear on top of earlier growth while both investors continue adding monthly contributions.

screens.title: What Creates the Advantage?
screens.question: What gives Hana an advantage when Omar begins at age 30?

options.text: Her investments are guaranteed to rise
options.response: Starting early does not guarantee positive returns. Investment values can rise or fall.

options.text: She has contributed for ten extra years
options.response: Correct. Her earlier contributions have also had more time for potential growth.

options.text: Her £100 is worth more than Omar’s £100
options.response: Their monthly amounts are equal. The important difference is how long the money remains invested.
Catching up may be possible, but it can require larger contributions and still depends on uncertain returns.

screens.title: Follow Forty Years of Growth
screens.instruction: Move through ages 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60. Compare each investor’s contributions, illustrative growth, and total balance.

educationalAssumptions: Each contributes £100 at the end of every month after starting.
The activity uses an illustrative annual return of 5%, compounded monthly.
The return remains smooth and constant only to make the role of time easy to see.
Real returns do not arrive smoothly and may be positive or negative.
Fees, taxes, inflation, missed contributions, and currency changes are excluded.
Balances are rounded to the nearest pound.
These values are examples, not forecasts or guaranteed outcomes.
The activity is educational and does not recommend a real investment.

screens.title: Time Gives Growth More Chances
screens.content: You saw Hana’s contributions begin working ten years sooner. This creates more time for compound growth, where returns may generate further returns. Starting early does not guarantee profit, and actual results depend on investment performance, fees, taxes, contribution consistency, and time invested. However, a longer time horizon can make modest contributions more powerful. Waiting may still be recoverable, but catching up can require much larger payments or a later goal date.
screens.simpleSummary: Starting earlier gives contributions and potential growth more time to build.
screens.illustration: Early contributions grow into branches, with later growth forming additional branches over a 40-year timeline.

screens.title: Starting With £50
screens.content: At 25, Mariam starts contributing £50 monthly to a fictional long-term investment. At 35, Sam begins the same amount. Mariam contributes more overall, but her earliest deposits also have ten extra years to potentially grow. Neither result is guaranteed.
screens.illustration: Two £50 monthly paths begin at ages 25 and 35, with the earlier path extending farther along the timeline.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on the advantage created by additional time in long-term investing.
The mission separates contributions from illustrative compound growth and clearly identifies the return assumption.
The mission uses monthly contributions, long-term goals, catch-up amounts, fees, taxes, and adult financial planning.
All contribution schedules, return assumptions, people, and balances are fictional educational examples.
The mission repeatedly states that the 5% classroom return and final balances are not guaranteed.
The mission does not discuss or predict the price of any real stock or investment.
Starting early, starting late, contributing small amounts, and pausing contributions are discussed without judgement.
The mission includes investment performance, fees, taxes, contribution consistency, inflation exclusions, and the uncertainty of real returns.
The mission uses pounds, monthly contributions, ages, employment income, and familiar long-term financial decisions.
The timeline separately displays contributions and illustrative growth at five ages and includes a later-start catch-up comparison.
The quiz addresses easy catch-up, small early contributions, guaranteed outcomes, and the importance of time.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, five slider milestones, five interaction questions, and three quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is practical, clear, respectful, and suitable for beginner adults.
